lead: For a lot of people, the Appalachian Trail is more than a path. It is the hike they took with their father at twelve, the section they walked on their honeymoon, the trip they talked about for thirty years and finally made. It is fog lifting off a bald in June, a fire tower at the top of a long climb, a quiet pond after a day on rocky ground.

When someone who loved those places dies, you can take them back one more time. Carry their ashes securely sealed in an unbreakable urn, walk the Trail together, and stand at the summit, the waterfall or the overlook they loved. Tell the stories, read the letter, take the photographs and celebrate the life you came to honor. That is the heart of this guide: one last amazing adventure.

The place where you say goodbye does not have to be the place where the ashes rest. Many of the Trail's most spectacular places are not open to scattering, or have no published rule. For every destination, we show you how to hold a meaningful remembrance there, and where the ashes can be scattered legally: sometimes at the same spot, sometimes at a nearby park that allows it, and sometimes only after you ask the land manager.

If you are still deciding where a loved one's ashes should go, our guides to scattering ashes in U.S. national parks and scattering ashes from a cruise ship cover two other paths families often choose.
rules: The Appalachian Trail is a single footpath, but it is not a single piece of land. The National Park Service administers a protected corridor, and the Trail also passes through seven National Park Service units, six national forests, and many state parks, state forests, game lands and smaller public and private parcels. Whoever manages the ground under your feet sets the rule.
That is why one overlook can allow scattering while the summit a few miles away does not, or has no published rule at all.

The Appalachian Trail Conservancy, the nonprofit that coordinates care of the Trail, does not own most of this land and has not published a position on scattering ashes. Its Leave No Trace guidance asks hikers to leave natural and historical objects where they find them, which is a good guide for any ceremony.

The national forests along the Trail have not published rules on scattering ashes either, and some national forests elsewhere in the country say it is not authorized. That is why every national forest place in this guide is marked Unconfirmed, and why we give the ranger district to call.
classifications: Permitted. The land manager publishes conditions under which you may scatter without a permit. You still have to follow every condition.
Permit or permission required. You need a permit, a letter, or approval before the ceremony.
Prohibited. The land manager says it is not allowed, or not allowed without official approval.
Unconfirmed. We could not find a published rule. That does not mean it is allowed. Call before you plan anything.
remembrance: Think of each trip in two parts. The remembrance is the adventure itself: the walk, the view, the words you share. The scattering is the moment the ashes are released, and it must happen where the land manager allows it. At a few places on the Trail, like the Shenandoah summits, the Blue Ridge Parkway and Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the two can happen together under the park's conditions. Everywhere else, keep your loved one's ashes sealed in an unbreakable urn during the ceremony and bring them back with you, then scatter them at a verified location or once the land manager has given permission.
npsRules: The remains must be cremated and pulverized.
Scatter on the ground, well away from trails, roads, buildings and water.
Spread the ashes so they do not collect in one place.
Leave nothing behind: no marker, urn or container.
Large groups or formal ceremonies may need a separate permit.
npsLead: If your chosen destination permits ash scattering, the following guidelines will help you plan a respectful ceremony. Specific requirements vary by location.
The exact distances and steps differ by park, and they are listed with each destination below.
leaveNoTrace: Even where scattering is allowed, the land comes first. Stay on durable ground, keep fragile plants like the grasses of the high balds untouched, carry out everything you carry in, and choose a quiet moment when other hikers are not nearby.
planning: Plan the remembrance and the scattering separately. Decide where you will gather, and where the ashes will be scattered legally. Ask the land manager first wherever no rule is published, and keep the answer in writing.
Choose your group size carefully. Several parks set a limit of 25 people before a permit is required.
Prepare the remains. National Park Service rules require cremated remains to be pulverized. Ask your funeral home or crematory if you are unsure.
Bring a scattering container you will carry home. Nothing may be left behind.
Watch the wind and the water. Stand so the wind carries ashes away from your group, and keep the required distance from streams, ponds and waterfalls.
Plan for the hike. Check the weather, seasonal road closures and parking limits. Carry water, layers and a map.
Think about everyone in the group. Several places in this guide, like Wayah Bald, Thundering Falls and the Pochuck Boardwalk, let older family members take part without a hard climb.
finalWord: A place on the Appalachian Trail can hold a whole life's worth of memories. Taking someone there one last time, and doing it in a way that respects the land and the people who care for it, is a gift to them and to every family who comes after you.

This guide is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by the National Park Service, the USDA Forest Service, the Appalachian Trail Conservancy or any state agency. Rules change. Always confirm with the land manager before you plan a ceremony.
quickAnswer: The Appalachian Trail runs through 14 states, and many of public agencies manage the land it crosses. There is no single rule for scattering ashes on the Trail. Shenandoah National Park, the Blue Ridge Parkway and the National Park Service's own Appalachian Trail lands allow it without a permit under strict conditions. Great Smoky Mountains National Park and Harpers Ferry require permission. New York State Parks do not allow it unless the state approves. For most national forests and state lands along the Trail, no published rule could be found, so the only safe answer is to ask the land manager first.

states.heading: Georgia
intro: The Trail begins in the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. We could not find a published Forest Service rule on scattering ashes for this forest, so every Georgia destination in this guide is Unconfirmed: a place for the remembrance, with the ashes kept sealed in an unbreakable urn, brought back with you and scattered where it is allowed.

states.heading: North Carolina
intro: North Carolina's Trail destinations here are in the Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests. Neither forest has a published rule we could find, so each is Unconfirmed. Hold the remembrance on the mountain, and scatter on the nearby Blue Ridge Parkway or in the Smokies, where the rules are published.

states.heading: Tennessee and the Great Smoky Mountains
intro: The Trail follows the Tennessee and North Carolina state line through Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The park allows scattering with a free Letter of Permission that you download from the park's website and carry with you. The park publishes two sets of distances. Its Letter of Permission (July 2026) asks you to stay 300 feet from buildings, towers, historic sites and cemeteries, 150 feet from roads, trails, campgrounds and picnic areas, and 150 feet from water. The park's own rulebook, the Superintendent's Compendium (updated June 2026), lists 200 feet, 100 feet and 150 feet for the same places. Following the letter's distances satisfies both, and the park can answer questions at (865) 436-1200. No birds, butterflies or other objects may be released, and a group of more than 25 people needs a Special Use Permit.

states.heading: Virginia
intro: Virginia holds more of the Trail than any other state, and three National Park Service units with clear, published rules.

Shenandoah National Park allows scattering without a permit: pulverized remains, on the ground at least 100 feet from any trail, road, developed facility or water, spread so they do not collect, no scattering from the air, and nothing left behind. A permit is needed for ceremonies or gatherings that might affect park operations. The park entrance fee applies. Call (540) 999-3500 with questions.

The Blue Ridge Parkway allows scattering without a permit for groups of 25 or fewer, pulverized, at least 100 feet from trails, roads, developed facilities and water. It is not allowed at Craggy Gardens, Devils Courthouse or Rough Ridge. Call 828 348-3400.

states.heading: West Virginia: Harpers Ferry
intro: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park allows scattering only with a special use permit and only in three designated areas: the Shenandoah River shoreline at the Point, the Potomac River shoreline at Potoma Wayside, and the vegetation next to Jefferson Rock. The park does not give exact points, and neither do we. Scattering ashes is one of the activities the park lists as needing a special use permit. The park's permit page says a non-refundable $50 application fee is due when you apply, that applications should arrive at least one month before the event, and that processing can take up to 30 days. The permits office is at 304-535-6232.

states.heading: Maryland
intro: Maryland's Department of Natural Resources says it is not legal in Maryland to spread ashes on public lands, so the Maryland state park destinations are remembrance places only. The nearby C&O Canal National Historical Park, run by the National Park Service, allows scattering with its free letter permit: notify the permits office in advance, receive a permit number, and stay at least 50 feet from the towpath, roads, trails and the Potomac River.

states.heading: New Jersey
intro: We could not find a published New Jersey State Park Service rule on scattering ashes, so the New Jersey destinations are Unconfirmed. They are wonderful places for the remembrance; ask the park office before planning to scatter.

states.heading: New York
intro: New York State Parks does not allow ashes to be released in state parks unless the Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation officially approves.

states.heading: Connecticut
intro: We were not able to confirm the land manager or a scattering rule for any Connecticut destination in this research, so none is listed yet. Great Falls at Falls Village and Lions Head remain candidates for a future update.

states.heading: Maine
intro: The Trail ends at Baxter State Park. We could not find a published Baxter rule on scattering ashes either way. Plan the remembrance in the park, and call Park Headquarters before planning to scatter.

description: Springer Mountain is where the Appalachian Trail begins.
